title: Force Diagrams and Forces on Moving Objects
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Physics
summary: Draw force diagrams that show the name, size and direction of each force, and use balanced and unbalanced forces to predict whether an object stays still, speeds up, slows down or changes direction.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Draw and use force diagrams that show the **name**, the **size** (in newtons) and the **direction** of each force acting on an object (6Pf.03).

Describe what different forces do to an object that is **at rest** (still) and to an object that is **already moving**: start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, change its direction or change its shape (6Pf.04).

blocks.text: 1. What is a force?

A **force** is a **push** or a **pull**. You cannot see a force, but you can see what it does: a force can make a still object start to move, make a moving object go faster, slower or change direction, and it can change an object's shape (squash, stretch, bend or twist it).

Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**, named after the scientist Isaac Newton. We measure a force with a **forcemeter** (also called a newton meter): a spring inside stretches more when the pull is bigger, and a pointer shows the force on a scale in N.

blocks.text: 2. The forces you need to know

rows: Always straight down, towards the centre of the Earth
On every object, all the time
An apple falls from a tree
When an object rests on or presses on a surface
A table holds up a book
Opposite to the movement (or the attempted movement)
When two surfaces slide or try to slide over each other
When an object moves through air
When an object moves through water
A swimmer feels the water pushing back
When an object is in water (or another liquid or gas)
The way you push or pull
When something or someone pushes or pulls
From an engine, a motor, legs or pedals
A car engine moves the car forwards

blocks.text: Notice the pattern: **friction, air resistance and water resistance always act against the movement.** If an object moves to the right, these forces point to the left. Air resistance and water resistance get **bigger when the object moves faster**, and they are smaller for **streamlined** shapes (smooth, pointed shapes like a fish or a racing car).
3. Drawing force diagrams
A **force diagram** shows every force on an object as an **arrow**. One arrow gives you three pieces of information at once.

blocks.text: **How to draw a force diagram — step by step**

items: Draw the object simply — a box or a circle is enough.

Think of **every** force acting on it: Is gravity pulling it down? Is a surface pushing it up? Is it moving (friction or air/water resistance)? Is something pushing or pulling it? Is it in water (upthrust)?
Draw each force as a straight arrow drawn with a ruler. The arrow **starts on the object** and **points the way the force acts**.
Make the **length** match the size: a force twice as big gets an arrow twice as long. Forces that are equal get arrows of the same length.
**Label** every arrow with its name and size, for example "weight 6 N".

blocks.text: 4. Balanced and unbalanced forces
Most objects have more than one force acting on them. To find what will happen, work out the **overall force** (also called the resultant force).

items: Forces in the **same direction**: **add** them. Two people pushing a car forwards with 200 N and 150 N give 350 N forwards.
Forces in **opposite directions**: **subtract** the smaller from the bigger. The overall force acts in the direction of the **bigger** force.
If the opposite forces are **equal**, the overall force is **0 N** and the forces are **balanced**.
If the overall force is not zero, the forces are **unbalanced**.

blocks.text: 5. What forces do to objects at rest and in motion

rows: It **starts to move** in the direction of the overall force.
It **keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction** (steady speed). It does NOT slow down or stop.

Overall force **forwards** (with the motion): it **speeds up**.; Overall force **backwards** (against the motion): it **slows down** and may **stop**.; Overall force **sideways**: it **changes direction**.

blocks.text: Forces can also **change the shape** of an object: squeezing a sponge, stretching an elastic band, bending a ruler or kicking a football (the ball squashes for a moment).

blocks.title: The big idea most students get wrong
blocks.text: A moving object does **not** need an overall force to keep moving. If the forces on a moving car are balanced, the car keeps going at a **steady speed**. On Earth things usually slow down because friction and air resistance are acting — once the engine force matches them, the speed stays the same.

blocks.text: **Story of a skydive:** (1) She jumps — weight is much bigger than air resistance, so she speeds up. (2) As she gets faster, air resistance grows until it equals her weight — balanced, so steady speed. (3) She opens the parachute — air resistance suddenly becomes much bigger than weight, so she slows down. (4) As she slows, air resistance falls until it equals weight again — balanced, so a new, slower steady speed. (5) She lands — the ground gives a big upward force that stops her.

blocks.title: بالعربي — الفكرة الأساسية
items: القوة يا زقّ (push) يا شدّ (pull)، وبنقيسها بالنيوتن (N) بجهاز اسمه forcemeter.
في رسم القوى: كل قوة سهم — اتجاه السهم = اتجاه القوة، وطول السهم = مقدار القوة، ولازم تكتب اسم القوة ومقدارها جنبه.
قوى متزنة (balanced): الحاجة الواقفة تفضل واقفة، والحاجة اللي ماشية تفضل ماشية بنفس السرعة — مش بتقف!
قوى غير متزنة (unbalanced): الجسم يتحرك أو يسرّع أو يبطّأ أو يغيّر اتجاهه — في اتجاه القوة الأكبر.
الاحتكاك ومقاومة الهواء ومقاومة الماء دايمًا عكس اتجاه الحركة.

blocks.text: 6. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — An apple hangs still from a branch. Its weight is 1.5 N. Draw a force diagram for the apple. [2]

items: The apple is still, so the forces must be balanced.
Gravity pulls down: arrow pointing **down**, labelled **weight 1.5 N**.
The stalk pulls up: arrow pointing **up**, labelled **pull of the stalk 1.5 N**, the **same length** as the weight arrow.

blocks.text: **Answer:** two arrows starting on the apple, equal length, opposite directions, both labelled 1.5 N. **Common mistake:** drawing the up arrow shorter — then the apple would fall.

**Worked example 2** — Two children push a heavy box to the right with forces of 40 N and 35 N. Friction on the box is 60 N. The box starts still. (a) Work out the overall force on the box. Show your working. [2] (b) Describe what happens to the box. [1]

items: Pushes in the same direction add: 40 + 35 = 75 N to the right.
Friction acts the opposite way (left): 75 − 60 = **15 N to the right**.
(b) The forces are unbalanced, so the box **starts to move to the right**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** adding all three numbers (40 + 35 + 60 = 135 N). Friction is in the opposite direction, so it must be subtracted. Always give the **direction** with the size.

**Worked example 3** — Look at the car diagram in section 4 (driving force 900 N, friction + air resistance 600 N). (a) Describe the motion of the car. [1] (b) The driver lets the driving force fall to 600 N. Describe the motion now. [1] (c) The driver then brakes, and the backward force becomes 1500 N while the driving force is 0 N. What happens? [1]

rows: 900 N forward, 600 N back → 300 N forward
600 N forward, 600 N back → 0 N, balanced
The car **keeps moving at a steady speed** (it does not stop).
0 N forward, 1500 N back → 1500 N backwards

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Explain why a skydiver falls more slowly after opening her parachute. [2]

**Answer:** The parachute has a large surface area, so **air resistance increases** (1 mark). Air resistance becomes bigger than her weight, so the overall force is upwards and she **slows down** until air resistance equals weight again and she falls at a slower steady speed (1 mark). **Common mistake:** saying "gravity gets smaller" — her weight does not change.
**Worked example 5** — In a football match, give **four** different effects of forces on the ball, with an example of each. [2] (1 mark for two correct, 2 marks for four)

items: **Starts it moving:** a player kicks a still ball from the centre spot.
**Speeds it up:** a player kicks a slowly rolling ball harder.
**Slows it down / stops it:** friction from the grass; the goalkeeper catches it.
**Changes its direction:** a player heads the ball to the side.
**Changes its shape:** the ball squashes for a moment when it is kicked.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6 (investigation)** — Laila lets a toy car roll down the same ramp onto four different surfaces and measures how far it travels on each.

items: (a) Which surface gives the most friction? Explain. [1] → **Sandpaper**, because the car travelled the **shortest** distance, so the force slowing it was biggest.
(b) Name the independent variable. [1] → **the type of surface**.
(c) Give two things Laila must keep the same. [2] → same car, same ramp height (same starting point), same way of releasing the car (do not push it).
(d) Write a conclusion. [1] → **The rougher the surface, the more friction, so the shorter the distance the car travels.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking a moving object stops when the forces are balanced. Balanced forces on a moving object = **steady speed**.
Forgetting to give the **direction** of the overall force ("15 N" alone is not complete — write "15 N to the right").
Drawing friction or air resistance in the same direction as the motion. They always act **against** the motion.
Drawing arrows that do not touch the object, or all the same length when the forces are different sizes.
Labelling arrows with only a name or only a number — Checkpoint wants **both** ("air resistance 200 N").
Writing the unit as kg. Force and weight are in **newtons (N)**; mass is in kg.
Saying "gravity" gets smaller when a parachute opens. The weight stays the same; it is air resistance that changes.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Complete the force diagram:** add an arrow with the correct direction and length, then label it. Use a ruler and check lengths match the sizes.
**Name the force:** one-word answers such as friction, air resistance, upthrust, weight, gravity.
**Calculate the overall force** from two or three arrows — show the subtraction and write the direction.
**Describe the motion:** use the exact phrases "stays still", "starts to move", "speeds up", "slows down", "moves at a steady speed", "changes direction".
**Explain** questions (2 marks): give the force comparison (e.g. "air resistance is bigger than weight") AND the effect ("so it slows down").
**Investigation** questions: ramps, toy cars, parachutes of different sizes — expect variables, predictions, and a conclusion that uses the word friction or air resistance.

questions.q: What is the unit of force?
questions.e: Forces (including weight) are measured in newtons, N. Kilograms measure mass.

questions.q: Which force always acts **against** the movement of an object sliding along the ground?
questions.e: Friction acts between the surfaces in the opposite direction to the movement.

questions.q: (a) Work out the size of the overall force on the box.
questions.e: The forces act in opposite directions, so subtract: 30 − 12 = 18 N.

questions.p: A box is pushed across the floor.
questions.q: (b) In which direction does the overall force act? Write left or right.
questions.e: The bigger force (the 30 N push) points to the right, so the overall force of 18 N acts to the right.

questions.q: A football rolls across the grass. It slows down and stops. Which force makes it stop?
questions.e: Friction between the ball and the grass (plus a little air resistance) acts against the motion and slows the ball until it stops.

questions.p: A small boat moves across a lake.
questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 540 175" width="540" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><rect x="20" y="120" width="500" height="50" fill="#cfe6f7" stroke="none" stroke-width="0"/><line x1="20" y1="120" x2="520" y2="120" stroke="#1f5fae" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M200,95 L340,95 L320,130 L220,130 Z" fill="#fff4d6" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="240" y="70" width="50" height="25" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="340" y1="110" x2="427" y2="110" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="440,110 427,117 427,103" fill="#c0392b" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="1"/><text x="345" y="85" fill="#c0392b">engine force 500 N</text><line x1="205" y1="110" x2="148" y2="110" stroke="#1f5fae" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="135,110 148,103 148,117" fill="#1f5fae" stroke="#1f5fae" stroke-width="1"/><text x="195" y="85" text-anchor="end" fill="#1f5fae">water resistance 350 N</text></svg>
questions.q: (a) Work out the overall force on the boat.
(b) What happens to the speed of the boat?
questions.p: A small boat moves across a lake.
questions.e: The overall force (150 N) is forwards, in the direction of motion, so the boat speeds up.

questions.q: A skydiver is falling at a **steady speed**. Her weight is 650 N. Which statement is correct?
c: Air resistance is bigger than 650 N.
Air resistance is smaller than 650 N.
Air resistance is equal to 650 N.
questions.e: Steady speed means the forces are balanced, so air resistance up = weight down = 650 N.

questions.q: A cyclist stops pedalling on a flat road and slowly comes to a stop. One force slowing her is friction from the road. Name the force from the air that also slows her.
questions.e: Air resistance (also called drag) acts against her motion.

questions.p: Two teams play tug of war with a rope.
questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 540 160" width="540" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><line x1="150" y1="90" x2="390" y2="90" stroke="#b9770e" stroke-width="5"/><line x1="270" y1="65" x2="270" y2="115" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/><text x="270" y="55" text-anchor="middle" fill="#0f1b33">centre line</text><line x1="150" y1="90" x2="73" y2="90" stroke="#1f5fae" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="60,90 73,83 73,97" fill="#1f5fae" stroke="#1f5fae" stroke-width="1"/><text x="105" y="125" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1f5fae">Team A 450 N</text><line x1="390" y1="90" x2="461" y2="90" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="474,90 461,97 461,83" fill="#c0392b" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="1"/><text x="432" y="125" text-anchor="middle" fill="#c0392b">Team B 420 N</text></svg>
questions.q: (a) Work out the overall force on the rope.
questions.e: The teams pull in opposite directions: 450 − 420 = 30 N.

questions.p: Two teams play tug of war with a rope.
questions.q: (b) Which team wins: A or B?
questions.e: The overall force (30 N) acts towards Team A, the team pulling harder, so the rope moves towards Team A.

questions.q: A ball rests on the floor. Its weight is 4 N. Describe the force diagram you would draw for the ball (draw it on paper first). [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: an arrow pointing DOWN from the ball labelled weight (or gravity) 4 N. 1 mark: an arrow pointing UP from the bottom of the ball labelled support force (or push of the floor / reaction) 4 N, the SAME LENGTH as the weight arrow. Do not accept arrows of different lengths.
questions.e: The ball is at rest, so the forces are balanced: weight 4 N down and support force 4 N up, drawn the same length.

questions.q: A car moves along a straight road. The driving force is 2000 N and friction plus air resistance is also 2000 N. Omar says: "The forces are balanced, so the car will stop." Is Omar correct? Explain your answer. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: No / Omar is wrong. 1 mark: balanced forces on a moving object mean it keeps moving at a steady (constant) speed (in the same direction). Do not accept 'it slows down'.
questions.e: No. The overall force is 2000 − 2000 = 0 N. A moving object with balanced forces keeps moving at the same speed and in the same direction. It would only slow down if the backward force became bigger.

questions.q: Sami pushes a toy car and lets it go on a smooth wooden floor. Then he pushes it the same way on a thick carpet. Predict on which surface the car travels further, and explain why. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: (on the) wooden floor. 1 mark: the wooden floor is smoother so there is less friction (acting against the motion), so the car slows down less / more slowly. Accept reverse argument for carpet (more friction).
questions.e: The car travels further on the wooden floor. The carpet is rougher, so it gives more friction, which acts against the motion and slows the car down faster.

blocks.title: Remember
items: A force is a push or a pull, measured in **newtons (N)** with a forcemeter.
Force arrows show **name + size + direction**; longer arrow = bigger force; label every arrow.
Same direction → add; opposite directions → subtract, and the overall force acts the way of the bigger force.
Balanced: still objects stay still, moving objects keep a **steady speed**. Unbalanced: start, speed up, slow down or change direction.
Friction, air resistance and water resistance always act **against** the motion; forces can also change shape.
